doc.title: Geometric Deep Learning Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges

proposal.title: Geometric Deep Learning Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges
proposal.gist: Deep learning architectures can be unified and derived from first principles of symmetry and invariance, in the spirit of Klein's Erlangen Programme for geometry.
proposal.question: Deep learning architectures — what single geometric blueprint unifies CNNs, GNNs, and other neural networks? (a blueprint of symmetry, scale separation, and equivariance)

children.title: Title, authors, date

children.title: Preface
children.gist: Just as Klein's Erlangen Programme unified geometries through symmetry groups, this text unifies deep learning architectures through the same symmetry-based lens, calling the result Geometric Deep Learning.
children.question: Deep learning's many architectures — can one Erlangen-style symmetry principle unify them? (a historical analogy and a stated goal)

children.title: Notation
children.gist: A reference table of symbols used throughout the text, defining notation for domains, signals, groups, operators and geometric quantities.

children.title: Introduction
children.gist: Because most high-dimensional learning tasks are not generic but carry physical symmetries, exploiting those symmetries through a unified geometric framework explains and extends successful neural architectures.
children.question: Deep learning's success on structured data — why do symmetry priors make high-dimensional learning feasible? (a unifying argument)

children.title: Learning in High Dimensions
children.gist: Learning a generic function in high dimensions is cursed by exponentially many samples needed, so some extra regularity assumption, beyond smoothness, is required to make learning tractable.
children.question: High-dimensional function learning — why does smoothness alone fail to beat the curse of dimensionality? (a mathematical argument with examples)

children.title: Supervised Learning Setup
children.gist: Supervised learning is framed as estimating an unknown function from N i.i.d. samples drawn over a high-dimensional data space, by choosing a parametrised function class and minimizing expected loss on new samples.

children.title: Inductive Bias via Function Regularity
children.gist: Because neural networks can approximate almost any continuous function arbitrarily well, interpolating training data alone leaves the solution underdetermined, so learning must also minimize a complexity measure that favors smoother, simpler functions among those that fit the data.

children.title: The Curse of Dimensionality
children.gist: Classical regularity notions like Lipschitz or Sobolev smoothness require exponentially many samples as dimension grows, a curse only partly escaped by sparsity-promoting neural network priors assuming low-dimensional structure, motivating geometric priors exploiting the domain's spatial structure instead.

children.title: Geometric Priors
children.gist: Two principles, symmetry of the domain and separation of scales, let neural networks escape the curse of dimensionality, and together they yield a general blueprint of equivariant local layers plus invariant pooling.
children.question: Geometric priors — how do symmetry and scale separation together let networks like CNNs beat the curse of dimensionality, and what architecture results? (a blueprint with building blocks)

children.title: Symmetry and scale introduced
children.gist: Since generic high-dimensional learning is hopeless, structured data lets learners exploit symmetry and scale separation, treating inputs as signals forming a Hilbert space over a domain, as CNNs already do through shared filters and pooling.

children.title: Symmetries, Representations, and Invariance
children.gist: Symmetries form groups whose elements act on a domain and, via linear representations, on signals, and functions built on such signals can be invariant (unchanged by the action) or equivariant (transformed correspondingly), as seen in classification versus segmentation.

children.title: Isomorphisms and Automorphisms
children.gist: Different levels of structure on a domain (set, topology, metric, orientation) define different symmetry groups nested as subgroups, and isomorphisms between distinct objects must be distinguished from automorphisms, symmetries of an object with itself, as in graphs.

children.title: Deformation Stability
children.gist: Because exact symmetry groups fail to capture local or approximate invariances in noisy real-world data, stability is instead measured by bounding how much a function's output changes under small deformations of signals or of the domain itself, using cost or distance measures like Dirichlet energy or graph edit distance.

children.title: Scale Separation
children.gist: Fourier transforms reveal global frequency information but become unstable under small deformations, whereas multiscale wavelet decompositions localize signals in both space and frequency, giving approximately equivariant and deformation-stable representations that motivate hierarchical scale separation in learning.

children.title: The Blueprint of Geometric Deep Learning
children.sourceHeading: 3.5 The Blueprint of Geometric Deep Learning
children.gist: Combining symmetry, stability and scale separation yields a blueprint where nonlinear localized equivariant layers, composed and interleaved with coarsening, build rich stable representations, since purely linear invariant functions collapse to trivial group averages like a single color mean.

children.title: Geometric Deep Learning Blueprint
children.gist: The Geometric Deep Learning Blueprint formally defines four building blocks, linear equivariant layers, pointwise nonlinearities, local pooling that coarsens the domain, and a final global invariant pooling, composed to build invariant functions respecting a chosen symmetry group.

children.title: Different settings of Geometric Deep Learning
children.sourceHeading: Different settings of Geometric Deep Learning
children.gist: Geometric Deep Learning architectures split into settings where the domain stays fixed while signals vary, as in images, versus settings where the domain itself varies, as in graph classification, with the same blueprint instantiated differently per domain and symmetry group.

children.title: Geometric Domains: the 5 Gs
children.gist: Five families of domains, grids, groups, graphs, geodesics and gauges, each carry a distinct notion of symmetry that determines how convolution, Fourier analysis and stability must be defined on them.
children.question: The five geometric domains — what distinct symmetry structure does each of grids, groups, graphs, geodesics and gauges impose on building convolutions? (five domain-by-domain constructions)

children.title: Overview of the five domains
children.gist: The text names five domain families, grids, groups, graphs, geodesics and gauges, each defined by its own symmetry notion, and discusses them not in strict order of generality but to highlight concepts underlying the Geometric Deep Learning blueprint.

children.title: 4.1 Graphs and Sets
children.gist: Graphs model relations between nodes without a fixed ordering, so functions on them must be permutation invariant or equivariant, a principle illustrated first on sets and then extended to general graphs using local neighbourhood aggregation.

children.title: 4.2 Grids and Euclidean spaces
children.gist: Grids are graphs with special fixed adjacency structure, so unlike general graphs they require no permutation invariance but instead demand the stronger geometric prior of translation invariance, underlying vision, language and speech applications.

children.title: Circulant matrices and Convolutions
children.gist: On a ring graph with fixed node ordering, local equivariant filters become circulant matrices equivalent to discrete convolutions, and convolution is shown to emerge necessarily from translation symmetry since circulant matrices are exactly those commuting with the shift operator.

children.title: Derivation of the discrete Fourier transform
children.sourceHeading: Derivation of the discrete Fourier transform
children.gist: Because circulant matrices are jointly diagonalised by a shared eigenbasis, picking the shift operator's eigenvectors derives the discrete Fourier transform from first principles, explaining the Convolution Theorem and showing graph Fourier analogues lose the grid's directional, multi-dimensional structure.

children.title: Derivation of the continuous Fourier transform
children.sourceHeading: Derivation of the continuous Fourier transform
children.gist: Repeating the argument for continuous functions on the real line shows that complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of the translation operator with simple spectrum, so every translation-equivariant linear operator must be a convolution and the Fourier basis its universal eigenbasis.

children.title: 4.3 Groups and Homogeneous spaces
children.gist: Both convolution and the Fourier transform generalise beyond simple shifts to any locally compact group equipped with an invariant measure, since convolution can be understood as matching a signal against shifted copies of a filter via an inner product.

children.title: Recap: the five domains
children.gist: This is a short recap heading restating the chapter's title, Geometric Domains: The 5 Gs, with no further content of its own.

children.title: Group convolution
children.gist: Defining a group convolution as the inner product between a signal and a group-transformed filter yields outputs defined on the group itself rather than the original domain, and this construction is proven to be equivariant to the group's action generally.

children.title: Spherical convolution
children.gist: On the two-dimensional sphere acted on by rotations in SO(3), spherical convolution produces outputs living on the three-dimensional rotation group rather than the sphere itself, forcing later layers to process signals defined over the group, called the regular representation, with practical limits restricting convolution to small or low-dimensional domains.

children.title: 4.4 Geodesics and Manifolds
children.gist: Manifolds generally lack a global symmetry group like the sphere's, so convolution cannot be built by sliding a shared filter everywhere, but they still admit two useful invariances, metric-preserving deformation and local reference frame change, relevant to physics, graphics and structural biology.

children.title: Riemannian manifolds
children.gist: A Riemannian manifold is a locally Euclidean curved surface equipped with a smoothly varying inner product, the Riemannian metric, on its tangent spaces, letting lengths and angles be measured intrinsically and functions built from such intrinsic quantities be automatically invariant to distance-preserving deformations called isometries.

children.title: Scalar and Vector fields
children.gist: Signals on a manifold are formalised as scalar fields, real-valued functions of position, and tangent vector fields assigning a tangent vector to each point, both forming vector spaces equipped with inner products defined through the Riemannian metric and its induced volume element.

children.title: Intrinsic gradient
children.gist: Because manifolds lack a global vector space structure, the ordinary differential cannot be defined by adding an infinitesimal displacement to a point, so vector fields are instead characterised axiomatically as linear derivation operators satisfying constancy, linearity and the Leibniz product rule on scalar fields.

children.title: Scalar and Vector fields (continued)
children.gist: This is a brief repeated heading restating that vector fields form a vector space equipped with an inner product defined through the Riemannian metric, carrying no new content beyond the earlier section.

children.title: Intrinsic gradient (continued)
children.gist: Geodesics will be used to define parallel transport of tangent vectors between points, the exponential map linking the manifold to its tangent space, and geodesic distance, together enabling convolution-like operations built locally in the tangent space.

children.title: Parallel transport
children.gist: Because tangent vectors at different points live in different spaces and cannot be directly compared, parallel transport along a geodesic moves a vector from one tangent space to another while preserving its length and its angle to the curve's velocity, though the result depends on the path taken.

children.title: Exponential map
children.gist: The exponential map sends a tangent vector at a point to the endpoint reached by travelling along the unique geodesic in that direction for unit time, giving a local diffeomorphism from the tangent space to the manifold whenever the manifold is geodesically complete.

children.title: Geodesic distances
children.gist: The Hopf-Rinow Theorem shows that geodesically complete manifolds are complete metric spaces, letting one define the geodesic distance between two points as the length of the shortest connecting path, with the minimum always attained.

children.title: Isometries
children.gist: A diffeomorphism between manifolds is called a Riemannian isometry when it preserves the metric exactly, and the Myers-Steenrod Theorem shows this coincides on connected manifolds with preserving geodesic distances, motivating the related notions of metric dilation and distortion for approximate isometries used to bound function stability under domain deformation.

children.title: Intrinsic symmetries
children.gist: A self-diffeomorphism of a manifold that preserves its own metric or distance is an intrinsic symmetry called an isometry, and the collection of all such isometries forms a group, the isometry group, under composition.

children.title: Fourier analysis on Manifolds
children.gist: Defining the gradient and its adjoint divergence operator yields the Laplace-Beltrami operator, an intrinsic, self-adjoint, isotropic operator whose orthogonal eigenfunctions form a discrete Fourier-like basis that is provably the smoothest and optimal basis for representing signals on a compact manifold.

children.title: Spectral Convolution on Manifolds
children.gist: Spectral convolution, defined as multiplying Fourier coefficients of signal and filter, is intrinsic and isometry-invariant but computationally expensive and unstable under domain perturbation, so parametrising filters as polynomial transfer functions of the Laplacian avoids eigendecomposition and gives a more stable, local, spatial-equivalent construction.

children.title: Spatial Convolution on Manifolds
children.gist: An alternative spatial convolution matches a filter defined on the tangent space against the signal via the exponential map, but requires choosing a local frame or gauge at each point, which is generally neither unique nor globally smooth, causing instability near singularities despite practical workarounds.

children.title: 4.5 Gauges and Bundles
children.gist: Gauge symmetry generalises the tangent frame idea to any vector bundle, a family of feature spaces attached to each point of a base manifold, whose chosen frame or gauge determines a signal's numerical coordinates even though the underlying geometric object stays unchanged.

children.title: Tangent bundles and the Structure group
children.sourceHeading: Tangent bundles and the Structure group
children.gist: Changing a gauge applies an invertible matrix at each point, forming a structure group such as GL(s), O(s) or SO(s), and the RGB color channel example shows how functions like a 1x1 convolution must transform consistently under such gauge changes to preserve their meaning.

children.title: Gauge Symmetries
children.gist: Treating gauge transformations as symmetries means a function is gauge equivariant if its coordinate expression stays unchanged under re-gauging, and building such equivariant convolutions on vector fields requires first parallel-transporting vectors to a common tangent space before applying a filter satisfying a structure-group commutation condition.

children.title: 4.6 Geometric graphs and Meshes
children.gist: Meshes, triangulated discretisations of surfaces used in graphics and vision, sit between graphs and manifolds, carrying a metric from embedded edge lengths that lets intrinsic, isometry-invariant properties be defined much as on continuous Riemannian manifolds.

children.title: Laplacian matrices
children.gist: The mesh Laplacian, built from permutation-invariant neighbour aggregation like the graph Laplacian, can use cotangent edge weights that make it converge to the continuous Laplace-Beltrami operator under refinement and remain invariant to isometric deformations of the mesh's intrinsic metric.

children.title: Spectral analysis on meshes
children.gist: Because direct spectral filtering is unstable across different meshes representing the same surface, polynomial or rational transfer functions of the Laplacian give stable, efficient filters, and functional maps generalise correspondence between differently discretised meshes into spectral operators enabling remeshing-invariant learning.

children.title: Geometric Deep Learning Models
children.gist: Applying the geometric blueprint to each of the five domains recovers, as special cases, CNNs, group-equivariant CNNs, GNNs, Transformers, equivariant message passing, mesh CNNs, RNNs and LSTMs.
children.question: Popular architectures — how does each of CNNs, GNNs, Transformers, mesh CNNs and RNNs fall out of the same geometric blueprint? (eight architecture derivations)

children.title: Introduction to the models
children.gist: This chapter shows how applying the geometric blueprint to each domain recovers familiar architectures like CNNs, GNNs, Transformers, equivariant networks, mesh CNNs, and RNNs, ordered for ease of understanding rather than strict generality.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan.apan

children.title: 5.1 Convolutional Neural Networks
children.gist: Convolutional neural networks, the earliest example of the geometric blueprint, arise from local translation-equivariant linear operators built from filter generators, extended with multiple input and output channels.

children.title: Efficient multiscale computation
children.gist: CNNs gain multiscale structure by alternating convolution with nonlinear activations like ReLU and pooling operations that coarsen the grid, enabling larger receptive fields with fixed parameter counts per layer.

children.title: Deep and Residual Networks
children.gist: Deep residual networks reparametrise each layer as a small perturbation of previous features rather than a full transformation, which can be viewed as discretising a continuous dynamical system and eases training of very deep models.

children.title: Normalisation
children.gist: Normalisation layers, inspired by biological gain control that rescales signals using local mean and variance, substantially improve CNN training, though why they help remains only partially explained theoretically.

children.title: Data augmentation
children.gist: Because CNNs do not natively encode invariances like lighting or small rotations, data augmentation artificially adds transformed training examples, though this is less sample-efficient than building richer invariance directly into the architecture.

children.title: 5.2 Group-equivariant CNNs
children.gist: Group-equivariant CNNs generalise ordinary convolution from Euclidean grids to any homogeneous space by moving filters using the symmetry group's transitive action rather than only translating them.

children.title: Discrete group convolution
children.gist: Discrete group convolution is illustrated through 3D medical images with cubic rotation symmetry and DNA sequences with reverse-complement symmetry, both combining translations with an additional discrete symmetry group.

children.title: Transform+Convolve approach
children.gist: Group convolution can be implemented efficiently by creating pre-rotated or reverse-complement-transformed copies of a filter and then running ordinary translational convolution with each copy, producing equivariant stacked orientation channels.

children.title: Spherical CNNs in the Fourier domain
children.sourceHeading: Spherical CNNs in the Fourier domain
children.gist: Spherical CNNs implement convolution on the sphere and rotation group in the Fourier domain using spherical harmonics and Wigner D-functions, with fast transform algorithms making such multi-layer networks computationally efficient.

children.title: 5.3 Graph Neural Networks
children.gist: Graph neural networks realize the blueprint on graphs via permutation equivariance, and nearly all GNN layers in the literature reduce to three flavours—convolutional, attentional, and message-passing—differing in how much they let neighbourhood features interact.

children.title: 5.4 Deep Sets, Transformers, and Latent Graph Inference
children.sourceHeading: 5.4 Deep Sets, Transformers, and Latent Graph Inference
children.gist: When nodes come as an unordered set without any specified adjacency or ordering, architectures like Deep Sets and Transformers model varying degrees of interaction between elements within the same GNN framework.

children.title: Empty edge set
children.gist: Assuming no edges at all, each set element is processed by an identical shared function independently of the others, yielding the Deep Sets architecture, equivalent to a convolutional GNN with self-loops only.

children.title: Complete edge set
children.gist: Assuming instead a complete graph between all elements leads through the attentional GNN flavour to self-attention, so Transformers can be understood exactly as attentional GNNs operating over a fully connected graph with positional encodings supplying order.

children.title: 5.5 Equivariant Message Passing Networks
children.gist: Equivariant message passing networks treat spatial node coordinates separately from other features, ensuring outputs rotate, reflect, and translate consistently with the input molecule under the Euclidean group, by depending only on invariant pairwise distances.

children.title: Irreducible representations
children.gist: Irreducible representation methods decompose roto-translation transformations into block-diagonal Wigner D-matrices and build equivariant kernels mapping between such representations, as used in Tensor Field Networks, 3D Steerable CNNs, and the SE(3)-Transformer.

children.title: Regular representations
children.gist: Regular representation approaches, including recent Lie group methods like LieConv and LieTransformer, offer more general but computationally heavier equivariance by storing feature copies for every group element rather than reasoning directly about representations.

children.title: 5.6 Intrinsic Mesh CNNs
children.gist: Triangular meshes, the standard representation for 3D objects in computer graphics, motivated researchers in the mid-2010s to adapt successful CNN ideas into dedicated intrinsic architectures for mesh-structured data.

children.title: Geodesic patches
children.gist: Mesh CNN filters are built from geodesic patches, local polar coordinate systems defined by shooting geodesics from a point, historically computed via the Fast Marching algorithm and first used in Geodesic CNNs.

children.title: Isotropic filters
children.gist: Because the reference direction of a geodesic patch is arbitrary, one simple fix is isotropic filters that aggregate neighbour features independent of direction, though this discards directional information like edges.

children.title: Fixed gauge
children.gist: An alternative to isotropic filters is fixing a specific gauge, such as principal curvature directions used for deformable body shapes or intrinsic gradient-based gauges that remain robust even at flat or singular points.

children.title: Angular pooling
children.gist: Angular max pooling matches an anisotropic filter against a geodesic patch across all possible rotations and keeps the strongest response, implemented on meshes via discretised patch operators with learnable or fixed weighting functions.

children.title: Gauge-equivariant filters
children.gist: Gauge-equivariant filters let network features transform under an arbitrary representation of the rotation group rather than staying invariant, implemented via message passing that parallel-transports features before combining them with direction-dependent learned filter matrices.

children.title: 5.7 Recurrent Neural Networks
children.gist: When inputs arrive sequentially over time on a fixed domain such as video frames, brain meshes, or traffic networks, an encoder respecting the domain's symmetry first compresses each step before recurrent neural networks aggregate the resulting sequence.

children.title: SimpleRNNs
children.gist: The SimpleRNN computes a summary vector at each step from the current input and previous summary through a single shared fully-connected layer, unrolled through time for training via backpropagation through time.

children.title: Translation equivariance in RNNs
children.gist: By left-padding sequences with zeros and choosing an initial summary vector as a fixed point of the update function, RNNs can be shown to satisfy a genuine translation equivariance property under left or right shifts.

children.title: 5.8 Long Short-Term Memory networks
children.gist: LSTMs introduce a memory cell with learned input, forget, and output gates that control how much information is retained, overwritten, or exposed, directly addressing the vanishing gradient problem of SimpleRNNs.

children.title: Time warping invariance of gated RNNs
children.sourceHeading: Time warping invariance of gated RNNs
children.gist: Gated RNNs like the LSTM achieve invariance to time-warping transformations because their gates can be shown to fit the derivative of the warping function, explaining their strength at modelling long-range dependencies and motivating chrono initialisation.

children.title: Problems and Applications
children.gist: Across chemistry, biology, recommender systems, traffic, vision, games, language, medicine and physics, treating data by its natural grid, group, graph, geodesic or gauge structure drives today's most impactful machine learning systems.
children.question: Geometric Deep Learning in practice — which real-world problems have been transformed by matching models to the data's natural geometric domain? (a survey of application areas)

children.title: Overview of applications
children.gist: Because real-world data commonly carry invariances and symmetries, many of the 21st century's most popular machine learning applications are, often unrecognized, byproducts of Geometric Deep Learning principles and architectures.

children.title: Chemistry and Drug Design
children.gist: Since testing candidate drugs experimentally is too costly given roughly 10^60 possible molecules, graph neural networks enable virtual screening, as shown when one such network identified Halicin, a diabetes drug, as a potent antibiotic against resistant bacteria.

children.title: Drug Repositioning
children.gist: Drug repositioning, reusing already-approved drugs for new purposes, is cheaper than novel drug design, and graph neural networks modeling biochemical interaction networks, as in Zitnik et al.'s polypharmacy side-effect prediction, now advance this 'network medicine' approach including against COVID-19.

children.title: Protein biology
children.gist: Proteins fold from amino acid chains into 3D structures that determine their biological function, and graph and mesh-based neural networks, including AlphaFold and MaSIF, now predict structure, function, and protein interactions for applications like cancer immunotherapy design.

children.title: Recommender Systems and Social Networks
children.gist: Large-scale recommender systems and social networks pioneered graph representation learning through link prediction, with Pinterest's PinSage scaling to billions of edges and Fabula AI using graph neural networks to detect misinformation spread patterns.

children.title: Traffic forecasting
children.gist: Transportation networks, modeled as graphs with intersections as nodes and roads as featurized edges, enable estimated time of arrival predictions that matter enormously to navigation apps and delivery or ride-sharing businesses worldwide.

children.title: Graph neural networks
children.gist: Graph neural networks now power production estimated-time-of-arrival predictions at Google Maps and Baidu Maps, treating travel time estimation as a graph regression task over road network subgraphs with strong measured improvements.

children.title: Object recognition
children.gist: The ImageNet classification challenge drove early convolutional neural network development, with AlexNet's 2012 breakthrough spawning VGG-16, Inception, and ResNets, while related object detection and segmentation tasks produced R-CNN and SegNet.

children.title: Game playing
children.gist: Convolutional neural networks act as translation-invariant feature extractors in reinforcement learning on grid-like game states, powering DeepMind's AlphaGo, its successors AlphaGo Zero, AlphaZero and MuZero, and Agent57's mastery of all 57 Atari games.

children.title: Text and speech synthesis
children.gist: Text and speech synthesis, operating on one-dimensional grids, progressed from recurrent networks through dilated convolutions like WaveNet to Transformer architectures such as BERT and GPT-3, enabling human-like generated speech and text at scale.

children.title: Healthcare
children.gist: In healthcare, CNNs analyze grid-structured scans, mesh networks model organs as surfaces, graph networks represent brain functional connectivity and patient similarity networks, and electronic health records are analyzed as patient graphs to improve diagnosis.

children.title: Particle physics and astrophysics
children.gist: Particle physicists and astrophysicists, long forced to fit unordered collision and detector data into artificial grids, now use graph and equivariant neural networks to classify particle jets, detect neutrinos, and analyze cosmic radio and microwave signals.

children.title: Virtual and Augmented Reality
children.gist: Geometric Deep Learning methods built for virtual and augmented reality use mesh convolutional networks and geometric autoencoders to analyze and synthesize 3D body, face, and hand motion, enabling real-time mobile avatar creation later used commercially by Snap.

children.title: Historic Perspective
children.gist: The idea that symmetry organizes knowledge runs from ancient geometry through Klein, Noether and gauge theory in physics to the independent, converging twentieth-century histories of CNNs, GNNs and spectral graph methods that this text unifies.
children.question: Symmetry as an organizing idea — how did separate historical threads in mathematics, physics and machine learning converge on today's Geometric Deep Learning? (a historical narrative)

children.title: Symmetry through the ages
children.gist: Hermann Weyl's reflections on symmetry as a route to order and beauty trace an ancient lineage, from Sumerian design through Pythagorean and Platonic geometry to Kepler's early scientific analysis of snowflakes' six-fold structure.

children.title: Symmetry in Mathematics and Physics
children.gist: Group theory, founded by Galois and developed by Lie, Klein and Cartan, became mathematics' language for symmetry, while Noether showed every continuous symmetry implies a conservation law, and Weyl's gauge invariance later unified physics' fundamental forces.

children.title: Early Use of Symmetry in Machine Learning
children.sourceHeading: Early Use of Symmetry in Machine Learning
children.gist: Long before deep learning, researchers like Amari and Minsky and Papert studied invariant pattern recognition and its limits, inspiring Fukushima's biologically-inspired Neocognitron and ultimately LeCun's convolutional neural networks.

children.title: Graph Neural Networks
children.gist: Graph neural networks emerged gradually from 1990s work on tree and structure processing, through Gori and Scarselli's recurrent fixed-point formulation, culminating in the more trainable Gated GNN model incorporating modern recurrent gating mechanisms.

children.title: Computational chemistry
children.gist: Independently of general graph learning, computational chemists built graph-based models of molecules since the 1990s, with later advances in molecular fingerprinting and quantum-property prediction making GNNs central to drug discovery today.

children.title: Node embeddings
children.gist: Unsupervised node embedding methods like DeepWalk and node2vec, based on random walks, were later shown mathematically equivalent to matrix factorization and gave way to contrastive, mutual-information-based self-supervised GNN training methods.

children.title: Probabilistic graphical models
children.gist: Graph neural networks also arose from probabilistic graphical models, where treating nodes as random variables with conditional-independence structure let researchers align GNN computations with mean-field inference and belief propagation via distribution embeddings.

children.title: The Weisfeiler-Lehman formalism
children.gist: The Weisfeiler-Lehman graph isomorphism test sets a provable upper bound on ordinary GNNs' expressive power, inspiring injective-aggregation architectures like GIN that reach this limit, though continuous features demand multiple aggregators instead.

children.title: Higher-order methods
children.gist: Because standard GNNs cannot detect certain structural patterns like rings, researchers developed higher-order k-WL-based architectures, invariant tensor networks, and structural augmentations such as node identifiers to boost expressive power.

children.title: Signal processing and Harmonic analysis
children.gist: Harmonic analysis and computational neuroscience inspired theoretical explanations for CNNs' success, including Poggio's cortex-inspired M-theory, steerable pyramids for texture modeling, and Mallat's scattering transforms using fixed wavelet filters.

children.title: Signal Processing on Graph and Meshes
children.sourceHeading: Signal Processing on Graph and Meshes
children.gist: Spectral graph neural networks using graph Fourier transforms grew from graph signal processing research, while a parallel, decade-older tradition in computer graphics had already developed spectral shape descriptors and functional maps on meshes.

children.title: Computer Graphics and Geometry Processing
children.gist: Geometry-processing researchers built geodesic CNNs and their generalizations like MoNet and graph attention networks for meshes and point clouds, while fully-connected graph architectures such as Transformers emerged independently in language and simulation tasks.

children.title: Algorithmic reasoning
children.gist: Algorithmic reasoning research designs neural networks, especially GNNs aligned with dynamic programming, to preserve algorithmic invariants like preconditions and postconditions, enabling extrapolation to inputs unlike those seen in training.

children.title: Geometric Deep Learning
children.gist: The term 'Geometric Deep Learning' was coined in 2015 and popularized in a 2017 paper, with later collaborators adding Graphs, Groups, Gauges and finally Geodesics to form this text's organizing '5 Gs' framework.
